name: Gravity
visual_anchor: A bright red apple falling from a leafy tree toward a smiling child on green grass, with a soft glowing arrow pointing down to the ground, sunny sky, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Invisible pull that makes dropped things fall to the ground
Keeps our feet on the floor and the Moon circling Earth
Much weaker on the Moon, so astronauts can bounce high
Isaac Newton described it after wondering about falling apples

facts_and_myths.claim: Without air, a feather and a hammer fall at the same speed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Air slows the feather down. With no air in the way, gravity pulls both objects down equally fast.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both landed together.

facts_and_myths.claim: There is no gravity at all in space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gravity reaches far into space. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling around Earth together.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You would weigh about one sixth as much on the Moon as you do on Earth.

name: Magnetism
visual_anchor: A shiny red and silver bar magnet pulling paper clips and metal washers across a wooden table, with playful curved lines showing an invisible pull, bright classroom light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Invisible force that pulls on some metals
Lets notes and pictures stick to the fridge door
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole
Opposite poles attract while matching poles push apart

facts_and_myths.claim: Magnets stick to every kind of metal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Magnets pull strongly on iron, nickel and cobalt, but not on aluminum cans, copper or gold.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Earth itself acts like a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle points north.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cutting a bar magnet in half makes two smaller magnets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Each piece gets its own north and south pole, so you can never get just one pole alone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The northern lights glow when particles from the Sun are steered by Earth's magnetic field.

name: Friction
visual_anchor: A cheerful child sliding fast on smooth ice next to a child moving slowly across a fluffy rug, with tiny sparkles where shoes touch the floor, bright playful colors, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Force that slows things down when surfaces rub together
Rubbing your hands quickly makes them feel toasty
Much smaller on smooth ice than on rough carpet
Shoe treads and bicycle brakes depend on it

facts_and_myths.claim: Rubbing your hands together quickly makes them feel hotter.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Friction turns the energy of motion into heat, which is why rubbing palms helps on a cold day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Long ago, people made campfires by spinning a wooden stick fast against another piece of wood.

facts_and_myths.claim: Friction is always bad, and we would be better off without it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Without friction we could not walk, hold a pencil or stop a bike, because everything would slide.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Skaters glide easily because ice has a thin, slippery layer on its surface.

name: Static Electricity
visual_anchor: A giggling child holding a bright blue balloon above their head while their hair stands straight up toward it, tiny playful sparkles in the air, cozy living room, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Makes your hair stand up after rubbing a balloon on it
Can make a balloon cling to a wall
Sometimes gives a tiny zap when you touch a doorknob
Electric charge that builds up on a surface instead of flowing

facts_and_myths.claim: Rubbing a balloon on your hair can make it stick to a wall.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rubbing moves tiny charged particles called electrons onto the balloon, and that charge clings to the wall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Static zaps happen more often in dry winter air than on humid summer days.

facts_and_myths.claim: Static electricity and lightning are completely different things.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity jumping between clouds or from clouds to the ground.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbed amber could pick up feathers and bits of straw.

name: Mirror Reflection
visual_anchor: A smiling child making a funny face at a round mirror, with a bright beam of flashlight light bouncing off the mirror in a zigzag, colorful bedroom, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Lets you see your own face in the bathroom
Happens when light bounces off a smooth, shiny surface
Makes writing look back-to-front
Light bounces off at the same angle it arrives

facts_and_myths.claim: Some ambulances have their name written backwards on the front on purpose.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Drivers ahead can read the word correctly in their rear-view mirrors, because mirrors flip writing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon so scientists can bounce laser beams off them from Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mirrors make their own light.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mirrors only bounce back light that hits them. In a totally dark room, a mirror shows nothing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A periscope uses two mirrors so people can see over walls or out of submarines.

name: Echo
visual_anchor: A happy child cupping their hands and calling out across a sunny canyon, with soft curved sound ripples bouncing off the orange rock walls and returning, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Sound that comes back to you after you shout
Easy to hear in big empty halls, caves and canyons
Happens when sound waves bounce off a hard surface
Bats and dolphins use it to find food

facts_and_myths.claim: Bats can find insects in the dark by listening to echoes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bats make high squeaks and listen for echoes bouncing back, an ability called echolocation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Most bat squeaks are too high-pitched for human ears to hear.

facts_and_myths.claim: A duck's quack is the only sound that does not echo.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scientists tested this and found that duck quacks do echo. The echo is just hard to notice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sound travels about 343 meters every second through air at room temperature.

name: Sound Waves
visual_anchor: A child gently tapping a shiny drum while colorful rippling rings spread through the air toward a friend's ear, bright cartoon music room, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Made when something vibrates back and forth
Our ears catch them and our brain hears them
Can travel through air, water and even solid walls
Cannot travel through the empty vacuum of space

facts_and_myths.claim: Sound cannot travel through empty outer space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sound needs something to vibrate, like air or water. Space is almost empty, so it stays silent.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sound travels about four times faster in water than it does in air.

facts_and_myths.claim: Light and sound travel at the same speed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Light is far faster, which is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whales can send their low songs across huge stretches of ocean.

name: Evaporation
visual_anchor: A shrinking rain puddle on a sunny sidewalk with soft wisps of vapor rising toward a bright yellow sun, a smiling child in rain boots watching, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Why puddles disappear on a sunny day
Turns liquid water into an invisible gas
Happens faster when it is hot and breezy
The step in the water cycle that lifts water into the air

facts_and_myths.claim: Wet clothes dry faster on a sunny, breezy day.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Heat gives water energy to escape as vapor, and wind carries the moist air away.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sweating cools you down because evaporating sweat carries heat away from your skin.

facts_and_myths.claim: Water has to boil before it can evaporate.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water evaporates at any temperature. Even a cool puddle slowly vanishes into the air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sea salt is made by letting seawater evaporate in shallow ponds until only salt remains.

name: Condensation
visual_anchor: A tall glass of icy lemonade on a sunny picnic table, covered in sparkling water droplets on the outside, a curious child touching the glass, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Water drops that appear on the outside of a cold glass
Fogs up the bathroom mirror after a hot shower
Happens when water vapor cools and turns back into liquid
How clouds form high in the sky

facts_and_myths.claim: Drops on the outside of a cold glass come from the air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Invisible water vapor in the air cools when it touches the glass and turns into liquid drops.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Clouds are made of countless tiny water droplets formed by condensation.

facts_and_myths.claim: A cold glass is leaking when it gets wet on the outside.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The glass is not leaking. The drops form from water vapor in the surrounding air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You can see your breath on cold days because the vapor in it condenses into tiny droplets.

name: Melting and Freezing
visual_anchor: Split scene of a dripping strawberry ice pop on a sunny beach beside sparkling ice cubes forming in a blue tray on a snowy windowsill, bright cheerful colors, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Makes ice cream drip on hot days and puddles turn icy in winter
Change of state between a solid and a liquid
Chocolate, candle wax and butter go through it too
Happens to pure water at 0 degrees Celsius

facts_and_myths.claim: Water takes up more space when it freezes into ice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water expands by about one tenth when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top, so fish stay safe in the water below.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sprinkling salt on icy roads works by heating the ice up.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Salt does not heat ice. It lowers the freezing point of water, so the ice melts even when cold.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chocolate melts in your mouth because it melts at just below body temperature.

name: Buoyancy
visual_anchor: A colorful beach ball and a toy wooden boat bobbing on clear blue pool water while a small pebble rests on the bottom, soft upward arrows under the floating toys, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: The upward push that helps things float
Why a beach ball bobs on top of a swimming pool
Lets giant steel ships float on the ocean
Archimedes figured it out while climbing into a bath

facts_and_myths.claim: Huge steel ships can float even though a steel block sinks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A ship's hollow shape pushes aside lots of water, and that water pushes the ship back up.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Legend says Archimedes shouted "Eureka!" after noticing the bath water rise when he climbed in.

facts_and_myths.claim: Heavy things always sink and light things always float.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Floating depends on shape and density, not weight alone. A giant log floats while a tiny pebble sinks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Salty seawater pushes up harder than fresh water, so swimming in the sea feels floatier.

name: Photosynthesis
visual_anchor: A bright green sprouting plant in a sunny flowerpot with golden sunbeams shining onto its leaves and tiny sparkling bubbles of air floating up, cheerful garden background, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: How green plants make their own food
Needs sunlight, water and air
Happens mostly in leaves, using green chlorophyll
Takes in carbon dioxide and gives off oxygen

facts_and_myths.claim: Plants give off oxygen that people and animals breathe.
facts_and_myths.explanation: During photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tiny ocean plants and algae make a huge share of the oxygen on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Plants get their food by eating soil through their roots.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Roots take up water and minerals, but plants build their own food from air, water and sunlight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light and soaks up red and blue light.

name: Water Cycle
visual_anchor: A colorful cartoon landscape with a blue ocean, a smiling sun, fluffy clouds and gentle rain falling on green mountains, with soft circular arrows linking them, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Endless journey of water around our planet
Water rises from oceans, forms clouds and falls as rain
Includes evaporation, condensation and precipitation
Powered mostly by heat from the Sun

facts_and_myths.claim: The water on Earth today has been recycled for billions of years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Earth keeps reusing the same water over and over, so the water you drink is very old.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water, and only a small part is fresh.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rain is brand-new water made inside clouds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Clouds only gather water that evaporated from oceans, lakes and plants. No new water is made.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Plants add water vapor to the air through tiny holes in their leaves.

name: Electric Circuit
visual_anchor: A neat science-kit setup on a desk with a battery, colorful red and black wires and a small glowing bulb in a closed loop, a child's hand pressing a little switch, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A loop that lets electricity flow
Lights up a bulb when wires join it to a battery
A switch opens or closes it
Only works when the path is complete with no gaps

facts_and_myths.claim: A bulb only lights up when its circuit makes a complete loop.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Electricity must flow out and back to its source. A gap anywhere in the loop stops the flow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Copper is used in most wires because it carries electricity very well.

facts_and_myths.claim: Flipping a switch on adds new electricity to the wires.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A switch just closes a gap in the circuit, letting electricity flow through the completed path.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A lemon with a copper coin and a zinc nail stuck in it can make a tiny electric current.

name: Lever
visual_anchor: A child easily lifting a big friendly cartoon boulder using a long wooden plank balanced on a small triangle-shaped rock, sunny park background, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Stiff bar that tips on a turning point to lift things
Seesaws, bottle openers and crowbars use it
Its turning point is called the fulcrum
A longer arm lets you lift heavy loads with less push

facts_and_myths.claim: A longer lever makes lifting a heavy load easier.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pushing far from the fulcrum gives more turning power, so less effort lifts the same load.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Archimedes said that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the world.

facts_and_myths.claim: Levers create extra energy out of nothing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Levers trade distance for force. You push less hard, but you must push farther.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Your forearm works like a lever, with your elbow acting as the fulcrum.

name: Pulley
visual_anchor: A smiling child pulling a rope that runs over a shiny wheel at the top of a tree house, lifting a basket of toys upward, bright leafy backyard, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Wheel with a rope running around it
Used to raise flags to the top of a flagpole
Pulling down on the rope lifts a load up
Cranes and elevators use several of them working together

facts_and_myths.claim: Using several pulleys together makes heavy loads easier to lift.
facts_and_myths.explanation: More rope sections share the weight, so you pull with less force but over a longer length.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Elevators hang from strong steel cables that run over large pulley wheels.

facts_and_myths.claim: A single fixed pulley cuts the effort needed to lift something in half.
facts_and_myths.explanation: One fixed pulley mainly changes direction, letting you pull down to lift up. The effort stays about the same.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Archimedes is said to have moved a whole ship using a system of pulleys.

name: Wheel and Axle
visual_anchor: A bright red toy wagon with big round wheels joined by a silver rod, rolling along a sunny garden path with a teddy bear riding inside, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Round wheel fixed to a rod through its center
Found on bikes, wagons and cars
Doorknobs and steering wheels use it too
Turning the big part a little turns the thin rod with more force

facts_and_myths.claim: A doorknob is a kind of wheel and axle.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Turning the wide knob spins the thin rod inside, making it easier to move the latch.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some of the oldest known wheels were used by potters to shape clay, not to move carts.

facts_and_myths.claim: A wheel and axle only helps things roll along the ground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It also multiplies turning force, as in doorknobs, faucet handles and screwdrivers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wheeled rolling suitcases only became popular around the 1970s, long after cars were invented.

name: Inclined Plane
visual_anchor: A child pushing a box of colorful blocks up a gentle wooden ramp onto a low stage, with a steep staircase beside it for comparison, bright playroom, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Flat surface set at a slant
Wheelchair ramps and playground slides are examples
Lets you raise a load by pushing it along a longer path
A gentler slope needs less push but a longer trip

facts_and_myths.claim: A gentle ramp needs less push than a steep one to raise a load.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A gentle slope spreads the work over a longer path, so each push can be smaller.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mountain roads zigzag back and forth so cars can climb on gentler slopes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Using a ramp means you do much less total work.
facts_and_myths.explanation: You push with less force, but over a longer distance, so the total work stays about the same.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A screw is really an inclined plane wrapped around a pole.

name: Wedge
visual_anchor: A bright yellow triangle-shaped rubber doorstop holding open a blue door, with sunlight streaming into a cheerful hallway, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Thick at one end and thin at the other
Doorstops, knives and chisels use this shape
Splits things apart or holds things in place
Like two inclined planes put back to back

facts_and_myths.claim: Your front teeth work like wedges when you bite into an apple.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their thin, sharp edges push the food apart, just like a wedge splitting wood.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A zipper uses tiny wedges inside its slider to open and close the teeth.

facts_and_myths.claim: A blunt wedge splits wood just as easily as a sharp one.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A thin, sharp wedge focuses the push on a small area, so it cuts or splits much more easily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A ship's pointed front acts like a wedge, pushing water aside as it moves.

name: Screw (Simple Machine)
visual_anchor: A giant friendly cartoon spiral with a glowing ridge winding around a silver pole, next to a jar with a twist-on lid, soft pastel science-lab background, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Spiral ridge wrapped around a rod
Moves forward a little each time it turns
Jar lids and light bulbs use its threads to twist on
Really an inclined plane wrapped around a pole

facts_and_myths.claim: A jar lid uses screw threads to close tightly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The spiral ridges turn a twisting motion into a strong push, pulling the lid down snugly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Archimedes screw, a turning spiral inside a tube, has lifted water for over 2,000 years.

facts_and_myths.claim: A screw is a totally different machine from a ramp.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A screw is an inclined plane wrapped in a spiral. Following its thread is like walking up a winding ramp.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Spiral slides at playgrounds follow the same twisting idea as a screw thread.

name: Gears
visual_anchor: A colorful set of big and small toothed wheels locked together and turning, in bright red, blue and yellow, with a happy child cranking a handle, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Wheels with teeth around the edge
Their teeth lock together to pass along turning motion
Found inside clocks and bicycles
A big one turning a small one makes the small one spin faster

facts_and_myths.claim: Two gears that touch each other turn in opposite directions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When one gear turns clockwise, its teeth push the next gear the other way.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bicycle gears help riders pedal up hills more easily by changing how far each pedal turn goes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gears were only invented in modern times.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gears are ancient. The Antikythera mechanism from ancient Greece used dozens of bronze gears.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In a clock, gears make the minute hand turn twelve times for each hour-hand turn.

name: Coil Spring
visual_anchor: A shiny silver metal coil bouncing a small toy up into the air above a bright trampoline, with playful motion lines, sunny backyard, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Bendy coil of metal wire
Squishes down and bounces back
Found in trampolines, pogo sticks and clicky pens
Stores energy when stretched or squeezed

facts_and_myths.claim: A squeezed spring stores energy and releases it when let go.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pressing a spring stores energy in the bent metal, which pushes back when you let go.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A Slinky toy is a long, loose spring that can walk down stairs.

facts_and_myths.claim: A spring can be stretched any amount and always bounce back.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Stretched too far, a spring bends out of shape and stays stretched instead of springing back.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many mechanical watches and wind-up toys are powered by a tightly wound spring.

name: Primary Colors
visual_anchor: Three big splashes of red, yellow and blue paint on a white art table, with a smiling child mixing them with a brush into orange, green and purple, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Group of three main colors
Red, yellow and blue in a classic art class
Mixed together to make many other colors
Screens use red, green and blue light versions instead

facts_and_myths.claim: TV and phone screens make every color from red, green and blue light.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tiny red, green and blue dots glow at different brightness to create all the colors you see.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Shining red, green and blue light together makes white light.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mixing all your paint colors together makes white.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mixing many paints gives a muddy brown or near-black. Only mixing colored light can make white.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Color printers mix cyan, magenta and yellow ink, plus black, to print colorful pictures.

name: Solids
visual_anchor: A neat display of a wooden block, a shiny ice cube, a smooth gray rock and a toy brick on a bright table, with a magnifying glass nearby, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Keeps its own shape without a container
Ice, wood and rocks are examples
Its tiny particles are packed tightly and only wiggle in place
One of the three common states of matter

facts_and_myths.claim: Ice is the solid form of water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When water cools to 0 degrees Celsius, its particles lock into place and form solid ice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Diamond is the hardest natural material, made of carbon atoms locked tightly together.

facts_and_myths.claim: The particles inside a solid do not move at all.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Particles in a solid still jiggle in place. They just cannot slide past each other.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Glass feels very solid, but it is made by melting sand at extremely high temperatures.

name: Liquids
visual_anchor: Bright orange juice being poured from a glass jug into a round bowl and a tall cup, taking each container's shape, sunny kitchen counter, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Flows and can be poured
Water, milk and honey are examples
Takes the shape of whatever container holds it
Its amount stays the same even when its shape changes

facts_and_myths.claim: A liquid takes the shape of its container.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its particles are close together but can slide past each other, so it flows to fill any shape.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Honey and water are both liquids, but thick honey flows much more slowly.

facts_and_myths.claim: Liquids can easily be squeezed into a much smaller space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Liquids hardly squeeze at all, which is why hydraulic machines use liquid to lift heavy loads.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Water is the only common substance found naturally on Earth as a solid, liquid and gas.

name: Gases
visual_anchor: A bunch of colorful helium balloons floating up into a bright blue sky above a happy child at a park, with soft swirls of air drawn around them, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Usually invisible and spreads out everywhere
Fills up balloons and bubbles
Its particles zoom around far apart from each other
Has no fixed shape and fills any container completely

facts_and_myths.claim: The air around us is a mixture of gases.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of other gases like carbon dioxide.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Helium is lighter than air, which is why helium balloons float upward.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gases weigh nothing at all.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gases do have weight. A balloon full of air is slightly heavier than an empty one.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You can smell cookies baking from another room because gas particles spread through the air.

name: Atoms
visual_anchor: A glowing cartoon model with a bright round center and tiny colorful dots zooming around it in looping orbits, floating against a deep purple starry background, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Tiny building blocks of everything around us
Far too small to see, even with a school microscope
Has a center called the nucleus with electrons around it
Each element on the periodic table is one kind of it

facts_and_myths.claim: Atoms are mostly empty space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Almost all of an atom's mass sits in its tiny center, with lots of empty space around it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word atom comes from a Greek word meaning "cannot be cut".

facts_and_myths.claim: Atoms are the smallest things that exist.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Atoms are made of even smaller particles called protons, neutrons and electrons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A single human hair is roughly a million carbon atoms wide.

name: Crystals
visual_anchor: A sparkling cluster of clear and purple crystals with flat shiny faces glowing on a dark velvet cloth, with a magnifying glass beside them, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Sparkly solids with flat faces and sharp, neat edges
Salt, sugar and snowflakes are examples
Their atoms line up in a neat repeating pattern
Can grow slowly from a liquid as it cools or dries

facts_and_myths.claim: Every snowflake is made of ice crystals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Snowflakes form when water vapor freezes into ice crystals, usually with six sides.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: With an adult's help, you can grow sugar crystals at home on a string.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ordinary window glass is a kind of crystal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ordinary glass is not a crystal. Its atoms are jumbled instead of lining up in a repeating pattern.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Table salt crystals are shaped like tiny cubes.

name: Density
visual_anchor: A tall clear glass with colorful stacked layers of golden honey, blue water and yellow oil, a small toy duck floating on top, bright kitchen science table, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Explains why oil floats on top of water
Tells how much stuff is packed into a space
A brick has more of it than a sponge of the same size
Worked out by dividing mass by volume

facts_and_myths.claim: Oil floats on water because oil is less dense.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Oil packs less mass into the same space than water, so it rises and floats on top.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You can stack honey, water and oil in a glass to make colorful liquid layers.

facts_and_myths.claim: A heavy object is always denser than a light one.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Density is about how tightly packed something is. A big beach ball is less dense than a tiny marble.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float.

name: Surface Tension
visual_anchor: A tiny water strider bug skating on a calm green pond, its long thin legs making gentle dimples in the shiny water surface, a silver paper clip floating nearby, soft morning light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Makes the top of water act like a thin, stretchy skin
Lets water strider bugs skate across ponds
Why a glass can be filled slightly above its rim without spilling
Water molecules at the surface pull tightly on each other

facts_and_myths.claim: Water strider bugs can walk on water thanks to surface tension.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water's surface acts like a thin stretchy skin, and the bugs' light, water-repelling legs press without breaking through.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A carefully placed paper clip can float on water even though steel is denser than water.

facts_and_myths.claim: Adding soap makes water's surface tension stronger.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Soap actually weakens surface tension, which helps water spread out and soak into dirt on dishes and clothes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Real raindrops are not teardrop-shaped; surface tension pulls small ones into round balls.

name: Isaac Newton
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon scientist with long curly hair and an old-fashioned coat sitting under an apple tree, looking up curiously at a red apple, sunny English countryside, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: English scientist famous for a story about a falling apple
Described the force of gravity
Wrote three famous laws of motion
Used a glass prism to show white light holds all the rainbow colors

facts_and_myths.claim: Newton showed that white light contains all the colors of the rainbow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He passed sunlight through a glass prism and saw it spread into a band of colors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Newton also built one of the first working reflecting telescopes, using a curved mirror.

facts_and_myths.claim: An apple fell on Newton's head and gave him the idea of gravity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Newton said watching an apple fall made him wonder about gravity, but nothing says it hit his head.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An apple tree linked to Newton's story still grows at his childhood home in England.

name: Marie Curie
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon woman scientist with neatly tied-up hair and a long dark dress, smiling beside glass beakers and a softly glowing jar in an old science lab, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Scientist born in Poland who did her famous work in France
First woman to win a Nobel Prize
Discovered two new elements, polonium and radium
Only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences

facts_and_myths.claim: Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: She named the element polonium after Poland, the country where she was born.

facts_and_myths.claim: Marie Curie won her first Nobel Prize all by herself.
facts_and_myths.explanation: She shared the 1903 physics prize with fellow scientists Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Her daughter Irene Joliot-Curie also went on to win a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

name: Thomas Edison
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon inventor in a vest and bow tie holding up a glowing light bulb in a busy workshop full of wires and gadgets, cozy golden light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Famous American inventor linked to the light bulb
Invented the phonograph, which could record and play back sound
Made a long-lasting electric bulb that homes could use
Held more than 1,000 United States patents

facts_and_myths.claim: Edison invented a machine that could record and play back sound.
facts_and_myths.explanation: His phonograph from 1877 recorded sound on a cylinder, and he tested it by reciting "Mary Had a Little Lamb".
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He was nicknamed the Wizard of Menlo Park after the New Jersey town where his lab stood.

facts_and_myths.claim: Edison was the very first person to make an electric light bulb.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Others made earlier bulbs. Edison's team made a practical, long-lasting bulb that homes could use.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Edison's team tested thousands of materials before finding a filament that glowed for many hours.

name: Albert Einstein
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon scientist with fluffy white hair and a big mustache smiling in front of a chalkboard covered in swirly doodles of stars and clocks, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Scientist famous for wild, fluffy white hair
Came up with the theory of relativity
Wrote the famous equation E = mc squared
Won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect

facts_and_myths.claim: Einstein's ideas showed that time can pass at different speeds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Relativity shows time runs slightly slower for things moving very fast or near strong gravity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Einstein loved playing the violin and often played music while thinking.

facts_and_myths.claim: Einstein failed math at school.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He was excellent at math and had taught himself calculus by about age 15.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His ideas help GPS satellites keep accurate time, so maps show the right location.

name: Leonardo da Vinci
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon artist-inventor with a long gray beard and a soft cap sketching a flying machine in a notebook, surrounded by paintbrushes and wooden models, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Italian artist and inventor from the Renaissance
Painted the Mona Lisa
Filled notebooks with designs for flying machines
Often wrote his notes in backwards mirror writing

facts_and_myths.claim: Leonardo da Vinci wrote many notes backwards in mirror writing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He was left-handed and often wrote from right to left, so his notes read correctly in a mirror.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He sketched ideas resembling a helicopter and a parachute hundreds of years before they were built.

facts_and_myths.claim: Leonardo da Vinci built a working airplane and flew it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He designed flying machines on paper, but there is no record that he ever built one that flew.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre Museum in Paris, France.

name: The Wright Brothers
visual_anchor: Two friendly cartoon brothers in caps cheering as a wooden two-winged airplane lifts off over sandy dunes by the sea, bright blue sky, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Two American brothers who loved building things
Ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio
Made the first powered airplane flight in 1903
Flew near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina

facts_and_myths.claim: The first Wright airplane flight lasted only about 12 seconds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: On December 17, 1903, Orville flew about 120 feet in 12 seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Later that same day, Wilbur flew 852 feet in 59 seconds.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Wright brothers invented the first flying machine of any kind.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hot-air balloons and gliders flew earlier. The brothers made the first controlled, powered airplane flight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A tiny piece of their 1903 Flyer traveled to Mars on NASA's Ingenuity helicopter.

name: Galileo Galilei
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon astronomer with a short beard peering through a long brass telescope at a bright Jupiter and its four little moons in a starry night sky, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Italian astronomer who explored the night sky with a telescope
Discovered four large moons circling Jupiter
Saw mountains and craters on the Moon
Tested how objects fall and how pendulums swing

facts_and_myths.claim: Galileo discovered four moons of Jupiter.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1610 he spotted Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, now called the Galilean moons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A NASA spacecraft that explored Jupiter was named Galileo in his honor.

facts_and_myths.claim: Galileo invented the very first telescope.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Telescopes were first made in the Netherlands. Galileo built better ones and pointed them at the sky.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He noticed that a swinging pendulum keeps nearly steady timing, an idea later used in clocks.

name: Alexander Graham Bell
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon inventor with a big bushy beard speaking into an early wooden telephone, with gentle sound ripples traveling along a wire, cozy old workshop, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Inventor linked to the telephone
Born in Scotland, later lived in Canada and the United States
Received a famous telephone patent in 1876
Spent years teaching deaf students to communicate

facts_and_myths.claim: Bell's first telephone words were spoken to his assistant, Thomas Watson.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1876 Bell said "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you" over his new telephone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bell suggested answering the phone with "Ahoy!" instead of "Hello".

facts_and_myths.claim: Alexander Graham Bell invented the cell phone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bell worked on the wired telephone in the 1870s. Handheld cell phones came about a hundred years later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He also helped build record-setting hydrofoil boats that skimmed above the water.

name: Ada Lovelace
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon woman in an elegant 1800s dress writing notes beside a giant brass machine full of gears and number wheels, soft candle-yellow light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: English mathematician from the 1800s
Daughter of the poet Lord Byron
Worked with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine
Often called the first computer programmer

facts_and_myths.claim: Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1843 she published steps for Babbage's Analytical Engine to calculate special numbers called Bernoulli numbers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A computer programming language called Ada is named after her.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ada Lovelace programmed a modern electronic computer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Electronic computers did not exist yet. She wrote for a mechanical machine that was never fully built.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ada Lovelace Day celebrates women in science, technology and math every October.

name: Jane Goodall
visual_anchor: A friendly cartoon woman scientist with a blond ponytail and khaki shirt sitting quietly in a green forest, smiling at a curious young chimpanzee holding a twig, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: British scientist famous for her work with animals
Spent decades watching wild chimpanzees
Did her research at Gombe in Tanzania
Discovered that chimpanzees make and use tools

facts_and_myths.claim: Jane Goodall discovered that chimpanzees use tools.
facts_and_myths.explanation: She watched chimps strip leaves off twigs and poke them into termite mounds to fish out termites.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: She gave the chimpanzees names, like David Greybeard, instead of numbers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Chimpanzees eat only fruit and plants.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Goodall saw that chimpanzees also eat insects and sometimes meat, along with lots of fruit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: As a child, she loved a toy chimpanzee named Jubilee.
